amendments.because: Owner chose the simpler message: ready-to-run commands with paths and branch names broke on Windows and unusual branches
amendments.done_when: forge upgrade run in a fix worktree says to drop that fix and run forge upgrade from the main checkout, with the exact commands, and forge next names forge upgrade <release> when a newer Forge release exists than the repo pins.

done_when: forge upgrade run outside the default branch says in plain words to drop the current fix (if it is a Forge fix) and run forge upgrade <release> from the main checkout on the default branch, with no branch names or paths pasted into commands; forge next names forge upgrade <release> when a newer release exists than the repo pins.

known.title: Quote values before putting them into recovery commands
Leave the fix worktree before running its drop command on Windows
Account for the branch checked out in the main checkout
Distinguish Forge fixes from ordinary fix-prefixed branches
Standard: A path compared as text goes through json.dumps or as_posix

findings.body:
Gain 5, Work 1, Harm 4
Raise: Security. Case: normal use - an agent follows the printed recovery command while working on an untrusted branch or in an untrusted checkout path. The branch name is inserted unquoted into `forge fix drop`, and the checkout path is placed inside double quotes, which still allow shell command substitution. For example, a Git branch named `fix/$(id)` makes the shell execute `id` before Forge can reject the invalid fix name. Git permits shell-special characters in branch names. The release argument is also echoed before validation. See [GitHub's branch-name guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/dealing-with-special-characters-in-branch-and-tag-names?apiVersion=2022-11-28).
findings.title: Quote values before putting them into recovery commands

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 1, Harm 3
Raise: Functional. Case: normal use - a Windows user follows the printed commands from a clean fix worktree. The first command runs `forge fix drop` while its current directory is the worktree; `src/forge/task.py:898-905` then tries to remove that directory after publishing the dropped state. Windows locks a process's current directory against deletion, so removal fails and the command exits unsuccessfully after partially completing the drop. The instructions need to move out of the worktree before the drop. [Microsoft documents the current-directory lock](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-setcurrentdirectory).
findings.title: Leave the fix worktree before running its drop command on Windows

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 1, Harm 3
Raise: Functional. Case: normal use - a fix is started while the main checkout is on a feature branch. `forge fix start` permits this (`src/forge/task.py:690-705`), but after dropping the fix, these instructions only change directory and rerun upgrade. The main checkout is still on the feature branch, so upgrade refuses again. If it is on another `fix/` branch, it instead recommends dropping that other fix. A managed fix can also be checked out in the main checkout itself, which `fix_drop` deliberately keeps on that branch (`src/forge/task.py:902-903`), causing the same recovery loop.
findings.title: Account for the branch checked out in the main checkout

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 1, Harm 3
Raise: Functional. Case: normal use - an adopted repository has an ordinary Git branch such as `fix/login` that was not started by Forge. This prefix check replaces the previous switch-to-default advice with `forge fix drop login`, but that command requires a matching Forge fix record and refuses with `Fix login has not started` (`src/forge/task.py:818-826`). The user no longer receives a usable recovery command.
Adds work: identify Forge-managed fixes before selecting the drop advice; F 2 x H 2 = 4; 2 x C = 2
findings.title: Distinguish Forge fixes from ordinary fix-prefixed branches

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 1, Harm 3
Raise: Test. Case: normal use - an agent starts a real Forge fix and requests an upgrade without naming a release. The test creates only a Git branch, with no Forge fix record, so the printed drop command cannot actually drop its fixture. A regression that handles only unmanaged branches could therefore pass while real fixes receive the old refusal. The omitted-release assertion at line 49 also matches the opening `forge upgrade runs on...` sentence even if the actual retry command is missing. Finally, line 48 rejects equivalent safe shell quoting, such as single quotes.
findings.title: Gate: test_1_upgrade_in_fix_names_drop_and_main_checkout

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 1, Harm 3
Raise: Gate. Case: normal use - a developer runs the repository's test command on Windows. The test interpolates a native `Path`, which uses backslashes, but the command prints the Git worktree path with forward slashes, so the assertion fails for both client fixtures. This breaks the stated rule: "A path written into a file or compared as text goes through json.dumps or as_posix."
findings.title: Standard: A path compared as text goes through json.dumps or as_posix

why: In a client repo, an agent asked to upgrade Forge runs forge fix start, but forge upgrade refuses in that fix's worktree, so the agent drops the fix and starts again (issue #1483).
